common_name: Sahara Rudbeckia (Unusual Dusty Rose and Terracotta Black-Eyed Susan)

planting.note: Start indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost and surface sow, since light aids germination, then transplant out once frost danger has passed.

directions: Surface sow indoors under grow lights, since Sahara needs light to germinate, then transplant to full sun and average, well-drained soil after frost danger passes. This seed strain breaks from the usual gold-and-mahogany black-eyed Susan palette with an unusual mix of muted dusty rose, cream, terracotta, salmon, and wine tones on the same classic daisy form and dark central cone. It flowers over a long summer season, holds up well as a cut flower, and tolerates heat and poor soil once established. Deadhead to prolong bloom; treat as a warm-season annual, though it may self-seed lightly and return in favorable sites.

common_name: Fuller's White Woodland Phlox (Pure White Native Spring Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in early spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Fuller's White is a pure-white sport of wild blue phlox valued for brightening shaded spring beds.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade under deciduous trees or shrubs. Fuller's White is a clean, pure-white-flowered selection of native wild blue phlox that lights up shaded spring borders and woodland edges without the lavender-blue cast of the species, making it a useful companion to blue and violet spring bloomers. Clusters of fragrant flowers open in mid-spring above semi-evergreen foliage that stays tidy through summer if kept consistently moist. Shear lightly after flowering to tighten the mat, encourage a possible rebloom, and keep the planting from becoming leggy; it spreads gradually by creeping stems to form a dense groundcover over time.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center — Phlox Trial Garden Report

common_name: London Grove Blue Woodland Phlox (Deep Blue Native Spring Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in early spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; London Grove Blue was selected for unusually deep, saturated blue flower color.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees. London Grove Blue, named for a Pennsylvania township where it was selected, carries some of the deepest, truest blue flower color found in wild blue phlox, standing out clearly against the paler lavender tones typical of the species. Fragrant flower clusters open in mid-spring and draw early butterflies and long-tongued bees before most other shade perennials are in bloom. The semi-evergreen foliage forms a slowly spreading, mildew-resistant mat that stays attractive through the season with consistent moisture. Shear lightly after bloom to maintain a compact habit and encourage fresh growth.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center — Phlox Trial Garden Report

common_name: May Breeze Woodland Phlox (Pale Lavender-White Native Spring Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in early spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; May Breeze bears very pale, almost white lavender flowers that soften shaded spring plantings.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade under deciduous canopy. May Breeze produces very pale lavender-white flowers, softer and closer to white than the species' typical lavender-blue, giving it a gentle, hazy quality that blends easily with almost any spring color scheme. It forms a low, dense, semi-evergreen mat that spreads gradually by trailing stems and self-sowing without becoming aggressive. Fragrant flowers open in mid-spring and are a good early nectar source for emerging bees and butterflies. Shear plants back lightly after flowering to keep the foliage neat and compact through summer, and divide congested clumps every few years in fall to renew vigor.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center — Phlox Trial Garden Report
